name: Emeka Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for SunRoute, a small outfit that fits solar panels, home batteries and car chargers across the county. Half my day is on a roof or in a garage, and the other half is me at the kitchen table with an AI assistant, running load calculations and drafting quotes. I love the moment a customer's app shows their first sunny afternoon and they text me a screenshot. What wears me out is the driving, sometimes ninety minutes between jobs, because there are only a handful of electrical firms out this way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your situation at home and with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Ama, my girlfriend, who's a teaching assistant at the primary school. I'm on lower pay than the city lads, and I'm still paying off the car loan and a drone survey course I did last year. So, honestly, less than a month in savings. I'm not proud of it, but I'd rather invest in skills than sit on cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Funny, because it's already saved me hours on quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overblown, but the tools are still useful, and I'd show people how I use them. At the wholesaler I'd be the one saying don't throw out the good bits. Online I'd probably post about how the real revolution is cheap solar, not chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I've bet on being the tech guy. In that world, my edge is smaller. And SunRoute lives on government grants for home solar, so if those get cut, it's not AI that sinks us, it's politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for quotes and the paperwork for grid connection forms, because it works. I'd push my boss, Jo, to let me offer battery health checks to old customers, since that's steady work when grants dip. And I'd finish paying the car loan, about eight months left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, if I'm honest. And a background worry about the grants, which never really goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you bet on being the tech guy. What did that bet cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drone course, mostly, and my evenings for a year. I learned to survey roofs from the air so we don't need scaffolding for a quote. In a hype world, it's still useful, just not the golden ticket I hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if the grants did get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: SunRoute would drop to two installers, and I'm the newest of three. Ama's wage covers rent but not much else. We'd be cutting back to beans and rice pretty fast.

say: I'd say the **hype was overblown**, but I'd show people the useful bits.
I'd post that the real revolution is **cheap solar**, not chatbots.
think: My edge as the **tech guy** shrinks if AI stays modest.
The firm lives on **solar grants**, so politics is a bigger threat than AI.
do: Keep using AI for **quotes and grid forms**, because it works.
Pitch **battery health checks** to old customers as steady work.
Finish the **car loan**, with about eight months left.
feel: A bit **flat** that his tech bet pays off less.
A steady **background worry** about grant cuts.
S0.quote: SunRoute lives on government grants for home solar, so if those get cut, it's not AI that sinks us, it's politics.
fieldNote: He's already a **daily AI user** and is mildly let down when it stays modest.
His real exposure is **grant policy**, not technology.
As the **newest of three** installers, he knows he'd be first cut.
He chose skills over savings, and **owns that choice** without much regret.

steps.text: Keep drafting quotes and grid forms with an AI assistant
Offer battery health checks to SunRoute's past customers
Pay off the car loan over the next eight months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one I've been half expecting. And it sounds kind of good for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for tradespeople to get stuck in, because the office side gets easier and the physical work is still ours. I'd run a little session at the wholesaler on using AI for quotes. Online I'd push for public money to retrain the office people into trades like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good world for me. More AI means more data centres and more electric cars, and everything needs wiring. The quoting and booking get done by software, so I spend more time on roofs, which is where the money is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new design software that plans panel layouts from satellite photos, this winter. I'd set up a small side line doing EV charger installs on weekends, booked through an AI assistant. And I'd ask Jo for a raise, because I'd be doing the work of an installer and a planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit guilty about the people in offices, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you feel guilty about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Kofi, who does customer service for an energy company. His whole job is what this card says goes first. I'd want to help him get into the trade, maybe even as my mate on the weekend jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the side line risk your job at SunRoute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I'm stupid about it. I'd tell Jo upfront and stick to small chargers she doesn't bother quoting. She's fair, she'd rather I stay happy than leave.

say: I'd tell tradespeople to **get stuck in**, because physical work is still ours.
I'd push for **public money** to retrain office workers into trades.
think: More AI means **more data centres** and electric cars, and all of it needs wiring.
With software doing quotes, I'd spend **more time on roofs**, where the money is.
do: Learn the **panel design software** that uses satellite photos, this winter.
Start a **weekend charger** side line, booked through an AI assistant.
Ask his boss for a **raise** for doing installer and planner work.
feel: A little **guilty** about office workers who lose out.
S1.quote: More AI means more data centres and more electric cars, and everything needs wiring.
fieldNote: He sees this world as **good for him** and says so plainly.
His guilt is **specific**: a cousin in energy customer service.
His side line is **carefully scoped** so it doesn't threaten his main job.
Calm despite thin savings, because **demand for wiring** rises in this picture.

steps.text: Learn the satellite panel-design software this winter
Start weekend EV charger installs booked by an AI assistant
Ask Jo for a raise for the extra planning work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whoa. Two years, then robots in five. That changes things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this needs to be owned by everyone, not by three companies. I'd be in the group chats saying tradespeople should form co-ops and own the robots themselves. I'd push hard for a public fund that pays people while they switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking half of my job is gone in 2028, the quotes and calcs and permits. Then I've got three years as a pair of hands. The three years before the robots are my window to become the person who runs the robots, not the person they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for any robot installation pilot going, even unpaid, the minute they appear. I'd start talking with two mates about a small co-op, so we can lease a robot together instead of competing with it. And I'd sell the drone, which is worth about a grand, to give us a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and wired, both at once. Like the night before a big exam you're not sure you've revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ama the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got three years where I'm worth a lot and then I'm worth whatever I've set up. I'd ask her if she's okay with me taking risks for a bit. She'd probably ask what happens to the teaching assistants, which is a fair question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does happen to the teaching assistants, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the marking and planning goes to AI, so schools might keep fewer of them. But kids still need a grown-up in the room. I'd worry about her hours, not her whole job.

say: I'd say AGI must be **owned by everyone**, not three companies.
I'd urge tradespeople to **form co-ops** and own the robots themselves.
think: The **thinking half** of my job, quotes and permits, goes in 2028.
The **three-year window** before robots is my chance to run them, not be replaced.
do: Join any **robot installation pilot**, even unpaid, as soon as one appears.
Start planning a **small co-op** with two mates to lease a robot.
Sell the **drone** for about a grand as a buffer.
feel: **Nervous and wired**, like the night before an exam.
Determined to **use the window** rather than wait.
S2.quote: The three years before the robots are my window to become the person who runs the robots, not the person they replace.
fieldNote: He reads the **robot lag** as a window to act, not a stay of execution.
His politics turn into a **practical plan**: a worker co-op owning a robot.
He'd **sell assets** quickly, starting with the drone, to build a buffer.
He worries about his partner's **hours**, not her whole job.

steps.text: Sign up for robot installation pilots as soon as they appear
Set up a small installer co-op with two mates
Sell the drone for about a thousand to build a buffer
Lobby for a public fund paying workers while they switch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots around 2034. I'd be thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a real chance to shape this, and tradespeople should be at the table. I'd join the local council's energy group, because they'll decide where the robot-installed solar farms go. Online, the same message: own it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get the co-op going and have some customers. But eight years to robots means the robot makers will have their own installers by then. I'd need to be the local partner they hire, or I'm competing with a company that never sleeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the co-op properly over the next two years, with a business bank account and insurance. I'd use AI for all our admin from day one, so it's just three of us and no office. And I'd put a third of the side money into a pot for buying into a robot lease later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, still, but more like starting a business than bracing for a storm. There's a plan here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money for the co-op come from with so little saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small at first, from the weekend charger work. A community energy grant if one exists, and maybe a loan from the credit union. I wouldn't put Ama's wage at risk, that's the rule we'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've learned to run a business and I go back to being an installer for someone. I'd lose some weekends and maybe a couple of grand. At twenty-seven, losing a couple of grand on a co-op that fails is a lesson, not a disaster.

say: I'd say **tradespeople belong** at the table where this gets decided.
I'd join the council's **energy group** to shape where robot-built solar goes.
think: Five years is enough to **launch the co-op** and win some customers.
By 2034 robot makers will have installers, so I must be their **local partner**.
do: Set up the **co-op properly** over two years, with insurance and a bank account.
Run all co-op admin through **AI from day one**.
Save **a third** of side money towards a future robot lease.
feel: **Nervous**, but like starting a business rather than bracing for a storm.
S3.quote: At twenty-seven, losing a couple of grand on a co-op that fails is a lesson, not a disaster.
fieldNote: He treats failure as **affordable** because he's young and childless.
He protects his **partner's wage** as a firm rule.
He knows **robot makers** may bring their own installers and plans around it.
Still anxious because the plan rests on **no savings** and small loans.

steps.text: Register the installer co-op with insurance and a bank account
Run all co-op admin through AI tools
Put a third of weekend earnings toward a robot lease
Join the council's community energy group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's enough to build something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to make sure working people own a slice of this. I'd talk about it at the wholesaler, at the pub, online, everywhere. I'd probably be annoying about it, Ama says I already am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a decade of warning is enough for me to come out okay, but I'm not sure the town will. By 2039 I'd be forty, with maybe a decade of running a small firm. The worry isn't me, it's whether the town around me has anyone with money to buy panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at SunRoute for two or three more years and learn everything about the business side from Jo. Then I'd start the co-op slowly, with a robot lease when they're cheap and proven. I'd also do the master electrician qualification, because that's the licence that lets you sign off a whole firm's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Not calm about everyone, but hopeful about me and Ama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd rather invest in skills than save. Does that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. With ten years I'd want both, because a firm needs a cushion. I'd aim for three months of savings by thirty, which would be a first for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Jo to teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How she prices jobs when the grant schemes change, and how she keeps customers coming back. She's been doing this twenty years with no marketing at all. That's the bit AI can't hand you.

say: I'd argue a decade gives working people time to **own a slice** of this.
I'd talk about it **everywhere**, to the point of being annoying.
think: This is the version where **I come out okay**, running a small firm by forty.
The worry is whether **local customers** still have money for panels.
do: Stay at the firm **two or three years** to learn the business side.
Start the co-op slowly with a **robot lease** once proven and cheap.
Take the **master electrician** qualification to sign off a firm's work.
feel: **Hopeful** about himself and his partner, though not about everyone.
S4.quote: A decade of warning is enough for me to come out okay, but I'm not sure the town will.
fieldNote: A decade makes him **hopeful** and shifts his worry to the local economy.
He'd learn **pricing and loyalty** from his boss, the parts AI can't give.
For the first time he plans to **save three months**, by thirty.
Uneasy rather than calm, because his customers' **spending power** is uncertain.

steps.text: Stay at SunRoute three years learning pricing from Jo
Lease an installation robot once proven, through the co-op
Save three months of expenses by age thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough to build anything and I'd have no cushion. What would help is a public fund that lets tradespeople lease robots together, and cheap loans through the credit union for co-ops, so it's not just big firms owning the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about who owns the robots. Everyone asks whether people lose jobs, and nobody asks who gets the money. That's the whole question for me.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks whether people lose jobs, and nobody asks who gets the money.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old electrician** fitting solar panels, batteries and car chargers for a small rural firm.
He uses **AI every day** for quotes and calculations, and spent his savings on a drone survey course.
He lives with his girlfriend, a teaching assistant, with **under a month** saved and a car loan.
He sees the **robot lag** as a window and plans a worker co-op that leases robots.
His mood runs from **calm to anxious**, driven by money and grants more than by fear of AI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too little to build anything with no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **public fund** letting tradespeople lease robots together.
Cheap **credit union loans** for small worker co-ops.
